MAYDAY - AIR TRAFFIC NAVIGATION SERVICES IN CRISIS

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We expose the growing risk in air safety in South Africa as a result of a crisis at the heart of the Air Traffic Navigation Service

Unique Selling Point:
We are able to pull together the complex picture of air safety in South Africa, narrated by industry players outside of the organisation charged with ensuring that safety, the ATNS, as well as from inside the agency which has been failing to meet its deadlines and is compromised by allegations of disfunction.

Summary:
It appears that South Africa’s safety guardians of the sky have been in trouble for some years – at least critically from 2017 when as the industry insiders say the “cracks began to show”.

However, those cracks became a chasm in July 2023 when vital safety instruments were suspended by the regulatory body the, the South African Civil Aviation Authority, SACAA.
https://www.caa.co.za.

These procedures create the legal route for aircraft to land and take-off from South Africa's airports, and if they are not properly sanctioned and administered, the safety risk increases dramatically, and in some instances, scheduled flights can not take off or land, causing delay and huge financial penalties to airlines and passengers, and the economy as a whole.



Further information:
This complex problem needs to be explained to be understood as it is a technical element of flying.

EXPLAINING PROCEDURES

All airplanes need to follow premapped routes to leave airports and land on them. These are called Procedures. There are IFP – Instrument Flight Procedures – and VFP’s Visual Flight Procedures/Rules.

International global agreements underpin the conventions of air safety and travel, and this way of mapping take-off and landing are part of those conventions and are called Procedures. Instrument Flight Procedures are conducted through the instruments in the cockpit. Visual Flight Procedures are from looking out of the window. And they are required to be renewed every five years. South Africa has 326 procedures for its main airports and in July 2023 they were suspended because they had expired.

The reason why they have to be renewed is because the terrain around the airports changes over time. And there needs to be a legal route that all airplanes take as they arrive and take off depending on the wind to ensure they don’t bump into each other or through pilot error they don’t crash in to anything. Until 2023, South Africa mostly had had these procedures in place.

The effect of NOT having these procedures in place is that if the weather is bad and a plane needs to land using one of these procedures, they will NOT be able to land and have to divert or circle, depending on how much fuel they have on board. The cost of diverting is potentially big, not just for the airline but also for the passengers who may be preparing to catch connecting flights, take a holiday, be at a meeting, deliver a widget, pharmaceuticals etc.

BACK TO THE STORY

The CAA then gave the ATNS an extension of a year to get their Procedures in order. They failed to come to the party and map those procedures. It appears that this failure was in part due to a toxic turmoil within the organisation which chased away skilled employees, and placed less skilled junior employees in their place.

Not only were Air Traffic controllers leaving in droves, but the people skilled enough to design the procedures were also leaving. Two whistleblower letters have been sent to the Minister of Transport and unions to complain about a raft of issues, which seem pretty standard in troubled SOEs – cronyism, incompetence, toxicity and a particular type of transformation which favours the well-connected. I have read the whistleblower letters – many of the commentators I have spoken to argue that they can not be relied on hundred per cent to tell the truth, but they are suggestive a basked of real problems. So much so that it attracted the attention of the Minister of Transport herself, Barbara Creecy.

A SOLUTION FOUND – AND THEN REJECTED

In the midst of the story which broke as a result of the ATNS missing its next deadline in July 2024, a solution was found in the appointment of a Swedish company which works in the Air Traffic Navigation Space Globally, IBG. https://ibg.aero This is a big professional global company with clients in the big flight centres of the world. The person they tasked to lead the pitch for work was a former South African air traffic controller, now in living in the UK, who has asked to be kept anonymous but with whom I spoke to this week.

IBG Aero offered to help train up the flight procedure designers that were there and help ATNS do all the procedures before the Christmas holidays. A contract was signed and a letter of appointment sent to them. But shortly after that happened, ATNS decided to do due diligence on its offering.

IBG sent them the names of the designers and their CVs. They came from SkyGuide which is the Swiss version of ATNS. The COO of ATNS, Josia Monyakoana, said they did not meet the standards that were required and rejected them. IBG sent the certificates of the designers they would deploy as proof of their abilities, and Mr Monyakoana said he did not trust the certificates, because they did not itemise the skills the designers had learnt on the courses which awarded them the certificates. So there was a series of to and fro with the IBG people – who had been to Johannesburg to prepare for the work – which has led to stalemate. All this I have now got from two sources, one of whom was in the negotiations.

WHY – DID THE CHIEF DESIGNER HAVE SOMETHING TO DO WITH IT?
While this was taking place, the newly appointed acting external Chief Designer of ATNS, Vuyo Kela, was setting up her own Aviation Consultancy company, while taking up the position of the most highly paid chief designer. She was a former employee of ATNS, had been working in Dubai, and had come back to South Africa looking for work. Josia Monyakoana was her referee on her CV of two years ago. The whistleblower letter alleges that Mr Monyakoana and Mr Kwela could be a romantic item, but I have no evidence of this. Nor have I found any trace of her company online, PWV Aviation Consultants, beyond her Linked In profile. So at this point, my evidence of this part of the story is hearsay, and what I am told off the record which is speculative and could be framed to some degree by the whistelblowers letters.

Two people I spoke to raised the issues of sexual harassment as part of the toxic culture of ATNS and how senior executives prey on younger women traffic controllers or staff. This is also mentioned in the whistleblower’s letters.

I have found evidence of this story in a recent scandal in Feb 2025 of ATNS air traffic boss demanding oral sex and other activities, including spanking, from a junior.
https://sundayworld.co.za/news/black-business-council-demands-suspension-of-sex-pest-boss/
https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/media-statement-sexual-harassment-allegations-under-investigation-gzkwf/?trackingId=CweG%2F12eTlaG52%2BV%2FpqZ5A%3D%3D
Apparently there are other incidences but nothing online that I can find.

The whistleblower’s letter list this and other issues building a case that ATNS has become dysfunctional and is run as a fiefdom of Josia Manyakoana and Vuyo Kwela.

The first whistleblower’s letter was released on the 18th of September 2024. It goes into detail giving the background of the people who were brought in by the new CEO, Nozipho Portia Mdawe, who came from Transnet National Ports Authority and knew very little about aviation. It complains that she brought in friends from Transnet, tried to get outside consultancies to compensate for the lack of knowledge of the highly paid newcomers, and pushed out expertise in the name of transformation. It concludes by calling for an investigation into 8 people who were appointed by Ms Mdawe and a number of other issues. The letter was addressed to the Minister Barbara Creecy and the unions and it was leaked to the media, all before the debacle with IBG.

As a result of the pressure, including quiet pressure from airlines, the Minister swooped in and suspended Ms Ndawo and sent in a three-person intervention team of former employees to try and stabilise the situation. There was a promise of the inclusion of a vendor (IBG of above) to help fix things and the less sceptical breathed a sign of relief.

But by March this year, it became clear that things were not fixing themselves despite all the hand holding. The Minister cranked up the pressure and held a press conference on the 14th of March at ATNS. She said she had now asked the intervention team to physically go into the offices daily. She claimed recruitment of procedure designers was going well and success was had in coaxing back procedure designers and flight controllers. Many have left for the Middle East or elsewhere in desperation. She herself appears to be taking personal responsibility for this as much as she can, within her ministerial ambit.

However, days after her press conference another whistleblower letter was released saying the Minister had had her facts wrong, that the ATNS was pulling wool over her eyes and that further symptoms of managerial dysfunction were undermining the work of the people who were meant to be keeping the aeroplanes and passengers safe.

One of the fights is over the unequal distribution of retainer bonuses across the country.

This last whistleblowers letter claims that:
In Nov 2024 Four Tower controllers left
In Dec 2024 Four radar controllers left
In Feb 2025 the tower pool manager left
More than six area controllers have left for Dubai

It’s difficult to properly quantify these numbers but it seems dire.

They also say that since Josia Manyakoana took over as COO five flight procedure specialist have left the company, with only one left, (and I think she has now left as well and is working as a consultant from outside)

Also the training has been delayed because there are only two instructors left and Vuyo Kela is allegedly refusing to hire in anybody, except her friends. She is apparently also managing recruitment and a number of other appointments.

At the same time, I have been told that the Presidency (not sure why) has added to the list of responsibilities of ATNS the job of mapping all the wind turbines in South Africa. They do not have the staff or capacity for this. It falls under Obstacle Evaluations. https://atns.com/uncategorized/wind-farm-application/8310/

There is now growing panic in the aviation services and the community around ATNS, although ATNS’s leaders are not necessarily expressing such. In a hastily convened meeting this week, ATNS leaders told airline executives that they had amended the procedures through an AMOC ( an alternative method of compliance) by writing notes to the maps, to give the airlines a route to land and take off at most of the airports. There is some doubt as to how legal that is, although an AMOC is a recognised procedure. There is concern that this has been done in order to make it possible for the G20 to land at George to go Fancourt for a meeting. Three airports have been left out – they haven’t got to their procedures yet – Bloemfontein, Upington and Richard’s Bay. That means scheduled aircraft can’t land if the weather is bad, if I read the press release correctly.

It also appears that the weather is often blamed for an ability of a plane to land, when in fact it is the case of the procedure being missing. If that procedure had been place, despite clouds, the aircraft would have landed.

While people have a lot to say about this off the record, it’s very difficult to get commentators to say all of this on the record. I have had enough off the record conversations to be convinced that ATNS is in serious trouble and that this is impacting on the safety and financial viability of the airline industry. But it’s not possible to test all those allegations in such a short period of time, and we would need a strategy to deal with the whistleblower’s report. There are a lot of angry airmen out there – and everybody is concerned. Except of course, it appears, the Chief Operating Officer himself, Josia Manyokoana and his Chief Designer, Vuyo Kela.

However our requests to interview Mr Manyakoana are being rebuffed and we have been given a lesser staff member to interview in Caine Mainganya. When I asked for an interview for the COO, Mr Manyakoana, for the third time in writing, I got this:

The COO is hands-on, overseeing the implementation of the entire ATNS Instrument Flight Procedure Maintenance Programme. It would be unfair to him to redirect his energies to something else, other than focusing in ensuring that our airspace is safe - at all times.

At the bottom of ATNS’s website it says:
We are always looking for talented people to join our organisation. Apply now and become part of our unique culture. Against these revelations, that seems ironic.

Press Release:


Mayday!
South Africa’s highly skilled air traffic officials have been leaving in droves as a crisis unfolds inside the agency tasked with keeping air travel safe. With thousands of aeroplanes flying across the country every day, what is the risk and cost to commercial airlines and their passengers? Carte Blanche investigates South Africa’s air safety procedures and the organisation that is failing to maintain them in time.

Script:


Soundup: Good morning ladies and gentlemen, we would like to welcome you on board and thank you for flying with us today. Please take your seats.

(VO1) DELAYS AT SOUTH AFRICAN AIRPORTS…
AND DIVERSIONS FROM LOCAL DESTINATIONS..
FLIGHT CANCELLATIONS ….AND A POSSIBLE CAUSE FOR AIRPLANE DISASTERS.
THE COMMERCIAL AVIATION INDUSTRY IS UP IN ARMS ABOUT A CRISIS AT THE HEART OF THEIR OPERATIONS.
THEY SAY IT’S NOT OF THEIR MAKING, NOR UNDER THEIR CONTROL.

Aaron Munetsi
CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa
We have an average of 35,000 passengers a month that are impacted by delays, diversions or canceled flights.

Miles van der Molen,
CEO, CemAir
And we feel overall that the system doesn't seem to have the capacity that's required for a busy airport like Johannesburg to move the traffic in and out of this airport every day.

Soundup: Ladies and Gentlemen, due to unexpected weather conditions our flight has been diverted.

(VO2) THE STATE-OWNED ENTERPRISE RESPONSIBLE FOR KEEPING US SAFE IN THE SKY IS BATTLING TO DO ITS JOB.

PIECE TO CAMERA MASA KEKANA:
THE AIR TRAFFIC NAVIGATION SERVICES OR ATNS IS THE SPECIALIST STATE AGENCY RESPONSIBLE FOR OVERSEEING THE FLOW OF AIR TRAFFIC.
IT MANAGES THE PEOPLE, THE TECHNOLOGY AND THE MAPS THAT GET PILOTS AND THEIR PASSENGERS FROM A TO B.
ATNS HAD A HISTORY OF EXCELLENCE - UNTIL ABOUT FOUR YEARS AGO WHEN THE CRACKS STARTED TO SHOW.

(VO3) IN JULY LAST YEAR, ATNS DROPPED THE BALL BADLY.
WITHOUT ANY PRIOR WARNING, ATNS TOLD AIRLINES THAT THEY HAD FAILED TO KEEP THEIR CHARTS UP TO DATE.
OVER THREE HUNDRED TECHNICAL MAPS WHICH ARE CALLED INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES OR IFP’S WERE WITHDRAWN, LEAVING PILOTS WITHOUT A CRITICAL TOOL REQUIRED FOR SAFE LANDING IN BAD WEATHER.


(VO4) THE CEO OF THE ASSOCIATION OF SOUTHERN AFRICAN AIRLINES AARON MUNETSI’S BEEN WATCHING THE DECLINE OF ATNS WITH ALARM - BECAUSE OF THE IMPACT ON AIRLINE FINANCES AND SAFETY.

MASA KEKANA: Can you compromise on airline safety in any way and if not, can you spell out why not?

Aaron Munetsi
CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa:
You definitely cannot. If you do, you're actually putting the lives of the operators, the pilots, the cabin crew and the passengers at risk. And if you are caught out, there's only one sanction. You are grounded. So most of the time, you'll find that airlines would rather cancel a flight if they, even for the slightest reason, believe that they cannot comply or adhere to the safety standards. The moment we think that we are not safe, we don't fly.

(VO5) WHICH IS WHY THE AIRLINES WERE APPALLED THAT SO MANY INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES WERE SUSPENDED AT ONCE.
KEEPING THEM UP-TO-DATE REQUIRES ROUTINE MAINTENANCE.
LETTING THEM EXPIRE ON THIS SCALE IS UNPRECEDENTED.
AND RISKY.


Aaron Munetsi
CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa:
One of the biggest costs for us as Airlines is obviously the insurance, because it's a it’s a regulatory requirement. So because we don't have this IFPS in place, the insurers get jittery. They start saying to us, mmh, ou're actually not that safe. Maybe we need to increase your premiums.

(VO6) A COCKPIT IS THE BEST PLACE TO UNDERSTAND HOW INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES WORK.
IFP’S HAVE TO BE REMAPPED EVERY FIVE YEARS TO FLAG NEW OBSTACLES IN THE TERRAIN THAT MIGHT ALTER A SAFE ROUTE FROM SKY TO GROUND.
VETERAN PILOT BOYD FICHARDT GAVE US A DEMONSTRATION IN A SIMULATOR.

MASA KEKANA: If you had to explain, you know, what IFPS are, what is needed for you to be able land and take off safely?

BOYD FICHARDT
CHIEF STANDARDS PILOT, CemAIr
This is effectively a road map in the sky. These charts allow pilots to get to certain altitudes above the ground safely, where, when they get to that stage, if they can see the runway, they can land. If they can't see the runway, we have to do what we call a go-around, which is where we have to abandon our approach. We've got certain altitudes that we are not allowed to go below unless we are exactly on this road map that is laid out for us.

BF: Now pull up a bit.

MK: Up a bit.
BF: Can you see that?

(VO7) FICHARDT SHOWS US HOW TO LAND UNDER A CLEAR BLUE SKY, USING GEORGE AIRPORT AS AN EXAMPLE.

BOYD FICHARDT
CHIEF PILOT, CemAir
If we did not have any approaches into George here at the moment, and these were the conditions we were faced with, Air Traffic Control would say to us, we are clear for the visual approach.Visual: can you see where you want to land? These conditions here, we can actually see the runway, so we will be able to land.The problem comes when we have cloud cover.

Voice: Thirty, twenty, ten.
BF: There we go.
MK: Woohoo!

BOYD FICHARDT SOUND UP: Alright Masa we have a three-hundred-foot cloud base here

(VO8) SO THEN IN OUR SIMULATION THE CLOUDS ROLL IN, WHICH IS COMMON IN WINTER IN GEORGE.
AND IT’S HERE THERE’S TROUBLE - BECAUSE WITHOUT VALID IFP’S, THE PILOTS CAN’T LAND IN BAD WEATHER.


BOYD FICHARDT
CHIEF PILOT, CemAir
When we get to this stage, we can not see the runway, we have to abandon the approach, well we have to fly away from the ground. Do we hold? Do we try again or in this case, this is not going to work for us, do we go to Cape Town?

(VO9) IN THE SIMULATOR, FICHARDT COULD THEN USE THE INSTRUMENT APPROACH TO BRING US DOWN TO LAND.
BUT IN REAL LIFE, WITHOUT OPERATIONAL IFPs, UNDER THESE CONDITIONS, A LANDING IS DENIED THE PLANE…AND ITS PASSENGERS.


(VO10) THE COST OF THESE DELAYS, CANCELLATIONS AND DIVERSIONS ARE IMMENSE.
THERE ARE REGULAR TRAFFIC QUEUES ON THE RUNWAY – OR IN THE SKY….
AN AIRPLANE BURNS TENS OF THOUSANDS OF RANDS OF FUEL AS IT QUEUES OR CIRCLES, WAITING TO LAND…
AND MORE TO DIVERT TO ANOTHER AIRPORT.

Aaron Munetsi
CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa
Since July 2024 up to January 2025 we had an equivalent of almost 400 diversions.

MASA KEKANA: And when that happens, is it the airline’s responsibility, as well, to refund, accommodate those passengers, if it's in another place?

Aaron Munetsi
CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa:
One hundred per cent, it’s our duty of care, our contract there with the passenger. 100% our responsibility. We do not recover this money from anybody.

(VO11) ATNS HAS BEEN SCRAMBLING TO GET THESE INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES RE-INSTATED WITH SOME SUCCESS, USING A HAND-AMENDED NOTICE TO AIRMAN OR AMOC TO UPDATE THE CHARTS.
BUT AIRLINE CHIEFS REMAIN ANGRY, INCLUDING THE OUTGOING CEO OF AIRLINK, RODGER FOSTER.

RODGER FOSTER: ATNS has created a serious safety risk, as airlines we are doing our best to mitigate it. Instrument flight procedures are fundamental to airline operational safety.

(VO12) FOSTER DELIVERED A SCATHING SPEECH AS HE RETIRED, SAYING THAT HIS AIRLINE HAD BLED R55 MILLION IN THE LAST YEAR AS A RESULT OF STATE DYSFUNCTION.
WE PUT THIS TO THE MINISTER OF TRANSPORT, BARBARA CREECY.

MASA KEKANA: It was the former Airlink CEO who lambasted ATNS. He basically called it economic sabotage.

BARBARA CREECY
Transport Minister, GNU
Yes, I saw his article.

MASA KEKANA: What did you make of that?

BARBARA CREECY
Transport Minister, GNU:
Well, he runs an airline. He's got a right to be angry.

MASA KEKANA: Do you understand where he's coming from as well, in that frustration?

BARBARA CREECY
Transport Minister, GNU:

AND CRITICALLY, SHE BACKED A RECRUITMENT DRIVE BECAUSE KEY PERSONNEL - IN PARTICULAR AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS - WERE LEAVING IN DROVES.

BARBARA CREECY
Transport Minister, GNU
South African Air Traffic controllers and also Flight Procedure Designers are extremely well trained, and they are in demand. And what we find is that developed countries can obviously offer much more in terms of packages than we are able to pay as a developing country.

IN PLACES LIKE DUBAI, THEY CAN EARN UP TO THREE TO FOUR TIMES A MONTH WHAT THEY ARE OFFERED IN SOUTH AFRICA.
IT’S A REASON WHY THIS YEAR’S WAGE NEGOTIATIONS IN ATNS WILL BE PARTICULARLY TOUGH, SAYS BAREND SMIT FROM THE LABOUR UNION SOLIDARITY.


BAREND SMIT
Union Representative, SOLIDARITY
The salaries have been lagging behind for years and years. We are working with the public safety here, this is air traffic control. I think holding nice little media conferences and stuff isn't really going to change anything. The shareholder should simply reach into its pockets and see what they can give to these people who are leaving and make a plan.

BETTER SALARIES ARE THE PULL – BUT THERE’S ALSO THE PUSH.

BARBARA CREECY
Transport Minister, GNU:
There was an organizational redesign process, which we have put on hold as a result of this intervention. We have been so focused on the crisis, I haven't had an opportunity to consider: was this a good process or a bad process? PIECE TO CAMERA MASA KEKANA:
WE HAVE HAD CONVERSATIONS WITH AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS WHO HAVE LEFT ATNS AND THEY HAVE CONFIRMED THE LOW MORALE, AS WELL AS THE DIFFICULTIES OF DOING THEIR JOBS BECAUSE OF BROKEN INFRASTRUCTURE AND POOR MANAGEMENT.

(VO16) ENTREPRENEUR MILES VAN DER MOLEN HEADS CEMAIR, A LOCAL AIRLINE WHICH TURNS TWENTY THIS YEAR.

ALL THIS HURTS HIS BOTTOM LINE.

MASA KEKANA: So if you're losing 10 million Rand in a matter of 12 months that wasn’t budgeted for, what has that done to your profits as an airline?

Miles van der Molen,
CEO, CemAir
Airlines across South Africa have always been very marginal, and can see that by the number of failures over the decades. So it is really damaging. Of course, you have to price it in ultimately to your ticket price. So ultimately, what will result in is higher cost of flying in the hands of the consumer.

MASA KEKANA: So more expensive tickets?

MILES VAN DER MOLEN: Absolutely prices have to go up if the costs go up, it’s simply how that couple works.

THERE’S A KNOCK-ON EFFECT ON MULTIPLE PARTS OF THE OPERATION - AND THE LIVES OF THE PASSENGERS AND AIRLINE CREW.

Miles van der Molen,
CEO, CemAir
If you have a severe delay in the morning and you may not be able to use the same crew as planned, you may need to get a new set of crew out to fly the aircraft for the later flight. (VO17)
WHEN WE FINALLY GOT TO SIT DOWN WITH THE ATNS BOARD CHAIRPERSON ZOLA MAJAVU, HE APOLOGISED TO AIRLINES AND THE PUBLIC.
AND THEN GAVE A STARTLING INSIGHT INTO THE LOW MORALE AT ATNS.

ZOLA MAJAVU
Board Chairman, ATNS
The board mandated me to do something unconventional, to descend to the level of operations, to say, you senior managers, get out of the way, maybe you are the reason why these people cannot talk. And I did station visits, and I spoke to all levels of management, and horrifying stuff was coming out. That place is toxic, it’s a snake pit. (VO18) AT THE MINISTER’S REQUEST, THE BOARD SUSPENDED THE CEO, NOZIPHO MDAWE, AND IS CONDUCTING A RANGE OF INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATIONS, ALONGSIDE A PROBE BY THE PUBLIC PROTECTOR.

MASA KEKANA: How did it get there?

ZOLA MAJAVU, Board Chair, ATNS: It's been like that, even before we came a year and a bit in there.

MASA KEKANA: So how do you clean up a toxic culture?

ZOLA MAJAVU: We have even resorted to not investigating using internal processes that are there in terms of your statutory labor law, because today it’s this one, tomorrow, it's that one. Today, I lay a grievance against you. You lay a counter grievance. It's a mess.

(VO19)OVER A LENGTHY INTERVIEW, MAJAVU AND HEAD OF OPERATIONS, CAINE MAINGANYA, PAINT A PICTURE OF AN SOE IN INTENSIVE CARE, GIVING A COMMITMENT THAT THEY ARE FIXING ATNS, WHATEVER IT TAKES.

ZOLA MAJAVU, Board Chair, ATNS:
Every single week the board submits a progress report to the Minister. I sign it every Monday because we want to keep our fingers on the pulse all the time because of complacency in some instances. We are making sure that we are keeping them on their toes, every week, every week.

(VO20) PART OF THIS RENEWAL IS AN AGGRESSIVE RECRUITMENT CAMPAIGN TO MAKE UP STAFF SHORTAGES, PARTICULARLY THE GAPS AT THE BUSIEST AIRPORTS

CAINE MAINGANYA
Head of Operations, ATNS
The example of OR Tambo, for example, we are sitting at about 70% staffing, We're sitting at about 80% staffing in Cape Town and in King Shaka, we also have made great strides at about 90% so those are generally the areas where we're seeing the most impact.

PIECE TO CAMERA MASA KEKANA:
SOUTH AFRICANS NEED TO FLY FOR BUSINESS AND PLEASURE
OUR ECONOMY DEPENDS ON IT.
AND THE AIRLINES ARE THE GEESE THAT DELIVER THE GOLDEN EGGS
AND THEY WANT TO BE HEARD…

MUNETSI SAYS MORE THAN A QUARTER OF ALL FLIGHTS ARE BEHIND TIME WHICH IS BAD FOR BUSINESS, UNDERMINES TOURISM AND THE ECONOMY IN GENERAL, AND THREATENS THE FUTURE OF THE AVIATION INDUSTRY.

Aaron Munetsi
CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa:
The airlines unfortunately bear the brunt. They are not compensated. The airlines also have to pay their air traffic navigation services fees. If they don't pay, they are grounded, so they pay the fees for a service that they don't receive.

MASA KEKANA: How is the industry coping with all this?

Aaron Munetsi
CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa:
We're a very resilient industry but we are really, really stretched to the max.

CEO, CemAir

Summary: It appears that South Africa’s safety guardians of the sky have been in trouble for some years – at least critically from 2017 when as the industry insiders say the “cracks began to show”. However, those cracks became a chasm in July 2023 when vital safety instruments were suspended by the regulatory body the, the South African Civil Aviation Authority, SACAA. https://www.caa.co.za. These procedures create the legal route for aircraft to land and take-off from South Africa's airports, and if they are not properly sanctioned and administered, the safety risk increases dramatically, and in some instances, scheduled flights can not take off or land, causing delay and huge financial penalties to airlines and passengers, and the economy as a whole. Further information: This complex problem needs to be explained to be understood as it is a technical element of flying. EXPLAINING PROCEDURES All airplanes need to follow premapped routes to leave airports and land on them. These are called Procedures. There are IFP – Instrument Flight Procedures – and VFP’s Visual Flight Procedures/Rules. International global agreements underpin the conventions of air safety and travel, and this way of mapping take-off and landing are part of those conventions and are called Procedures. Instrument Flight Procedures are conducted through the instruments in the cockpit. Visual Flight Procedures are from looking out of the window. And they are required to be renewed every five years. South Africa has 326 procedures for its main airports and in July 2023 they were suspended because they had expired. The reason why they have to be renewed is because the terrain around the airports changes over time. And there needs to be a legal route that all airplanes take as they arrive and take off depending on the wind to ensure they don’t bump into each other or through pilot error they don’t crash in to anything. Until 2023, South Africa mostly had had these procedures in place. The effect of NOT having these procedures in place is that if the weather is bad and a plane needs to land using one of these procedures, they will NOT be able to land and have to divert or circle, depending on how much fuel they have on board. The cost of diverting is potentially big, not just for the airline but also for the passengers who may be preparing to catch connecting flights, take a holiday, be at a meeting, deliver a widget, pharmaceuticals etc. BACK TO THE STORY The CAA then gave the ATNS an extension of a year to get their Procedures in order. They failed to come to the party and map those procedures. It appears that this failure was in part due to a toxic turmoil within the organisation which chased away skilled employees, and placed less skilled junior employees in their place. Not only were Air Traffic controllers leaving in droves, but the people skilled enough to design the procedures were also leaving. Two whistleblower letters have been sent to the Minister of Transport and unions to complain about a raft of issues, which seem pretty standard in troubled SOEs – cronyism, incompetence, toxicity and a particular type of transformation which favours the well-connected. I have read the whistleblower letters – many of the commentators I have spoken to argue that they can not be relied on hundred per cent to tell the truth, but they are suggestive a basked of real problems. So much so that it attracted the attention of the Minister of Transport herself, Barbara Creecy. A SOLUTION FOUND – AND THEN REJECTED In the midst of the story which broke as a result of the ATNS missing its next deadline in July 2024, a solution was found in the appointment of a Swedish company which works in the Air Traffic Navigation Space Globally, IBG. https://ibg.aero This is a big professional global company with clients in the big flight centres of the world. The person they tasked to lead the pitch for work was a former South African air traffic controller, now in living in the UK, who has asked to be kept anonymous but with whom I spoke to this week. IBG Aero offered to help train up the flight procedure designers that were there and help ATNS do all the procedures before the Christmas holidays. A contract was signed and a letter of appointment sent to them. But shortly after that happened, ATNS decided to do due diligence on its offering. IBG sent them the names of the designers and their CVs. They came from SkyGuide which is the Swiss version of ATNS. The COO of ATNS, Josia Monyakoana, said they did not meet the standards that were required and rejected them. IBG sent the certificates of the designers they would deploy as proof of their abilities, and Mr Monyakoana said he did not trust the certificates, because they did not itemise the skills the designers had learnt on the courses which awarded them the certificates. So there was a series of to and fro with the IBG people – who had been to Johannesburg to prepare for the work – which has led to stalemate. All this I have now got from two sources, one of whom was in the negotiations. WHY – DID THE CHIEF DESIGNER HAVE SOMETHING TO DO WITH IT? While this was taking place, the newly appointed acting external Chief Designer of ATNS, Vuyo Kela, was setting up her own Aviation Consultancy company, while taking up the position of the most highly paid chief designer. She was a former employee of ATNS, had been working in Dubai, and had come back to South Africa looking for work. Josia Monyakoana was her referee on her CV of two years ago. The whistleblower letter alleges that Mr Monyakoana and Mr Kwela could be a romantic item, but I have no evidence of this. Nor have I found any trace of her company online, PWV Aviation Consultants, beyond her Linked In profile. So at this point, my evidence of this part of the story is hearsay, and what I am told off the record which is speculative and could be framed to some degree by the whistelblowers letters. Two people I spoke to raised the issues of sexual harassment as part of the toxic culture of ATNS and how senior executives prey on younger women traffic controllers or staff. This is also mentioned in the whistleblower’s letters. I have found evidence of this story in a recent scandal in Feb 2025 of ATNS air traffic boss demanding oral sex and other activities, including spanking, from a junior. https://sundayworld.co.za/news/black-business-council-demands-suspension-of-sex-pest-boss/ https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/media-statement-sexual-harassment-allegations-under-investigation-gzkwf/?trackingId=CweG%2F12eTlaG52%2BV%2FpqZ5A%3D%3D Apparently there are other incidences but nothing online that I can find. The whistleblower’s letter list this and other issues building a case that ATNS has become dysfunctional and is run as a fiefdom of Josia Manyakoana and Vuyo Kwela. The first whistleblower’s letter was released on the 18th of September 2024. It goes into detail giving the background of the people who were brought in by the new CEO, Nozipho Portia Mdawe, who came from Transnet National Ports Authority and knew very little about aviation. It complains that she brought in friends from Transnet, tried to get outside consultancies to compensate for the lack of knowledge of the highly paid newcomers, and pushed out expertise in the name of transformation. It concludes by calling for an investigation into 8 people who were appointed by Ms Mdawe and a number of other issues. The letter was addressed to the Minister Barbara Creecy and the unions and it was leaked to the media, all before the debacle with IBG. As a result of the pressure, including quiet pressure from airlines, the Minister swooped in and suspended Ms Ndawo and sent in a three-person intervention team of former employees to try and stabilise the situation. There was a promise of the inclusion of a vendor (IBG of above) to help fix things and the less sceptical breathed a sign of relief. But by March this year, it became clear that things were not fixing themselves despite all the hand holding. The Minister cranked up the pressure and held a press conference on the 14th of March at ATNS. She said she had now asked the intervention team to physically go into the offices daily. She claimed recruitment of procedure designers was going well and success was had in coaxing back procedure designers and flight controllers. Many have left for the Middle East or elsewhere in desperation. She herself appears to be taking personal responsibility for this as much as she can, within her ministerial ambit. However, days after her press conference another whistleblower letter was released saying the Minister had had her facts wrong, that the ATNS was pulling wool over her eyes and that further symptoms of managerial dysfunction were undermining the work of the people who were meant to be keeping the aeroplanes and passengers safe. One of the fights is over the unequal distribution of retainer bonuses across the country. This last whistleblowers letter claims that: In Nov 2024 Four Tower controllers left In Dec 2024 Four radar controllers left In Feb 2025 the tower pool manager left More than six area controllers have left for Dubai It’s difficult to properly quantify these numbers but it seems dire. They also say that since Josia Manyakoana took over as COO five flight procedure specialist have left the company, with only one left, (and I think she has now left as well and is working as a consultant from outside) Also the training has been delayed because there are only two instructors left and Vuyo Kela is allegedly refusing to hire in anybody, except her friends. She is apparently also managing recruitment and a number of other appointments. At the same time, I have been told that the Presidency (not sure why) has added to the list of responsibilities of ATNS the job of mapping all the wind turbines in South Africa. They do not have the staff or capacity for this. It falls under Obstacle Evaluations. https://atns.com/uncategorized/wind-farm-application/8310/ There is now growing panic in the aviation services and the community around ATNS, although ATNS’s leaders are not necessarily expressing such. In a hastily convened meeting this week, ATNS leaders told airline executives that they had amended the procedures through an AMOC ( an alternative method of compliance) by writing notes to the maps, to give the airlines a route to land and take off at most of the airports. There is some doubt as to how legal that is, although an AMOC is a recognised procedure. There is concern that this has been done in order to make it possible for the G20 to land at George to go Fancourt for a meeting. Three airports have been left out – they haven’t got to their procedures yet – Bloemfontein, Upington and Richard’s Bay. That means scheduled aircraft can’t land if the weather is bad, if I read the press release correctly. It also appears that the weather is often blamed for an ability of a plane to land, when in fact it is the case of the procedure being missing. If that procedure had been place, despite clouds, the aircraft would have landed. While people have a lot to say about this off the record, it’s very difficult to get commentators to say all of this on the record. I have had enough off the record conversations to be convinced that ATNS is in serious trouble and that this is impacting on the safety and financial viability of the airline industry. But it’s not possible to test all those allegations in such a short period of time, and we would need a strategy to deal with the whistleblower’s report. There are a lot of angry airmen out there – and everybody is concerned. Except of course, it appears, the Chief Operating Officer himself, Josia Manyokoana and his Chief Designer, Vuyo Kela. However our requests to interview Mr Manyakoana are being rebuffed and we have been given a lesser staff member to interview in Caine Mainganya. When I asked for an interview for the COO, Mr Manyakoana, for the third time in writing, I got this: The COO is hands-on, overseeing the implementation of the entire ATNS Instrument Flight Procedure Maintenance Programme. It would be unfair to him to redirect his energies to something else, other than focusing in ensuring that our airspace is safe - at all times. At the bottom of ATNS’s website it says: We are always looking for talented people to join our organisation. Apply now and become part of our unique culture. Against these revelations, that seems ironic. Extra Budget Items: We will most likely need more flights than usual, because we will be shooting in PE and Johannesburg. South Africa’s highly skilled air traffic officials have been leaving in droves as a crisis unfolds inside the agency tasked with keeping air travel safe. With thousands of aeroplanes flying across the country every day, what is the risk and cost to commercial airlines and their passengers? Carte Blanche investigates South Africa’s air safety procedures and the organisation that is failing to maintain them in time. Script: Soundup: Good morning ladies and gentlemen, we would like to welcome you on board and thank you for flying with us today. Please take your seats. (VO1) DELAYS AT SOUTH AFRICAN AIRPORTS… AND DIVERSIONS FROM LOCAL DESTINATIONS.. FLIGHT CANCELLATIONS ….AND A POSSIBLE CAUSE FOR AIRPLANE DISASTERS. THE COMMERCIAL AVIATION INDUSTRY IS UP IN ARMS ABOUT A CRISIS AT THE HEART OF THEIR OPERATIONS. THEY SAY IT’S NOT OF THEIR MAKING, NOR UNDER THEIR CONTROL. Aaron Munetsi CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa We have an average of 35,000 passengers a month that are impacted by delays, diversions or canceled flights. Miles van der Molen, CEO, CemAir And we feel overall that the system doesn't seem to have the capacity that's required for a busy airport like Johannesburg to move the traffic in and out of this airport every day. Soundup: Ladies and Gentlemen, due to unexpected weather conditions our flight has been diverted. (VO2) THE STATE-OWNED ENTERPRISE RESPONSIBLE FOR KEEPING US SAFE IN THE SKY IS BATTLING TO DO ITS JOB. PIECE TO CAMERA MASA KEKANA: THE AIR TRAFFIC NAVIGATION SERVICES OR ATNS IS THE SPECIALIST STATE AGENCY RESPONSIBLE FOR OVERSEEING THE FLOW OF AIR TRAFFIC. IT MANAGES THE PEOPLE, THE TECHNOLOGY AND THE MAPS THAT GET PILOTS AND THEIR PASSENGERS FROM A TO B. ATNS HAD A HISTORY OF EXCELLENCE - UNTIL ABOUT FOUR YEARS AGO WHEN THE CRACKS STARTED TO SHOW. (VO3) IN JULY LAST YEAR, ATNS DROPPED THE BALL BADLY. WITHOUT ANY PRIOR WARNING, ATNS TOLD AIRLINES THAT THEY HAD FAILED TO KEEP THEIR CHARTS UP TO DATE. OVER THREE HUNDRED TECHNICAL MAPS WHICH ARE CALLED INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES OR IFP’S WERE WITHDRAWN, LEAVING PILOTS WITHOUT A CRITICAL TOOL REQUIRED FOR SAFE LANDING IN BAD WEATHER. (VO4) THE CEO OF THE ASSOCIATION OF SOUTHERN AFRICAN AIRLINES AARON MUNETSI’S BEEN WATCHING THE DECLINE OF ATNS WITH ALARM - BECAUSE OF THE IMPACT ON AIRLINE FINANCES AND SAFETY. MASA KEKANA: Can you compromise on airline safety in any way and if not, can you spell out why not? Aaron Munetsi CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa: You definitely cannot. If you do, you're actually putting the lives of the operators, the pilots, the cabin crew and the passengers at risk. And if you are caught out, there's only one sanction. You are grounded. So most of the time, you'll find that airlines would rather cancel a flight if they, even for the slightest reason, believe that they cannot comply or adhere to the safety standards. The moment we think that we are not safe, we don't fly. (VO5) WHICH IS WHY THE AIRLINES WERE APPALLED THAT SO MANY INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES WERE SUSPENDED AT ONCE. KEEPING THEM UP-TO-DATE REQUIRES ROUTINE MAINTENANCE. LETTING THEM EXPIRE ON THIS SCALE IS UNPRECEDENTED. AND RISKY. Aaron Munetsi CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa: One of the biggest costs for us as Airlines is obviously the insurance, because it's a it’s a regulatory requirement. So because we don't have this IFPS in place, the insurers get jittery. They start saying to us, mmh, ou're actually not that safe. Maybe we need to increase your premiums. (VO6) A COCKPIT IS THE BEST PLACE TO UNDERSTAND HOW INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES WORK. IFP’S HAVE TO BE REMAPPED EVERY FIVE YEARS TO FLAG NEW OBSTACLES IN THE TERRAIN THAT MIGHT ALTER A SAFE ROUTE FROM SKY TO GROUND. VETERAN PILOT BOYD FICHARDT GAVE US A DEMONSTRATION IN A SIMULATOR. MASA KEKANA: If you had to explain, you know, what IFPS are, what is needed for you to be able land and take off safely? BOYD FICHARDT CHIEF STANDARDS PILOT, CemAIr This is effectively a road map in the sky. These charts allow pilots to get to certain altitudes above the ground safely, where, when they get to that stage, if they can see the runway, they can land. If they can't see the runway, we have to do what we call a go-around, which is where we have to abandon our approach. We've got certain altitudes that we are not allowed to go below unless we are exactly on this road map that is laid out for us. BF: Now pull up a bit. MK: Up a bit. BF: Can you see that? (VO7) FICHARDT SHOWS US HOW TO LAND UNDER A CLEAR BLUE SKY, USING GEORGE AIRPORT AS AN EXAMPLE. BOYD FICHARDT CHIEF PILOT, CemAir If we did not have any approaches into George here at the moment, and these were the conditions we were faced with, Air Traffic Control would say to us, we are clear for the visual approach.Visual: can you see where you want to land? These conditions here, we can actually see the runway, so we will be able to land.The problem comes when we have cloud cover. Voice: Thirty, twenty, ten. BF: There we go. MK: Woohoo! BOYD FICHARDT SOUND UP: Alright Masa we have a three-hundred-foot cloud base here (VO8) SO THEN IN OUR SIMULATION THE CLOUDS ROLL IN, WHICH IS COMMON IN WINTER IN GEORGE. AND IT’S HERE THERE’S TROUBLE - BECAUSE WITHOUT VALID IFP’S, THE PILOTS CAN’T LAND IN BAD WEATHER. BOYD FICHARDT CHIEF PILOT, CemAir When we get to this stage, we can not see the runway, we have to abandon the approach, well we have to fly away from the ground. Do we hold? Do we try again or in this case, this is not going to work for us, do we go to Cape Town? (VO9) IN THE SIMULATOR, FICHARDT COULD THEN USE THE INSTRUMENT APPROACH TO BRING US DOWN TO LAND. BUT IN REAL LIFE, WITHOUT OPERATIONAL IFPs, UNDER THESE CONDITIONS, A LANDING IS DENIED THE PLANE…AND ITS PASSENGERS. (VO10) THE COST OF THESE DELAYS, CANCELLATIONS AND DIVERSIONS ARE IMMENSE. THERE ARE REGULAR TRAFFIC QUEUES ON THE RUNWAY – OR IN THE SKY…. AN AIRPLANE BURNS TENS OF THOUSANDS OF RANDS OF FUEL AS IT QUEUES OR CIRCLES, WAITING TO LAND… AND MORE TO DIVERT TO ANOTHER AIRPORT. Aaron Munetsi CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa Since July 2024 up to January 2025 we had an equivalent of almost 400 diversions. MASA KEKANA: And when that happens, is it the airline’s responsibility, as well, to refund, accommodate those passengers, if it's in another place? Aaron Munetsi CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa: One hundred per cent, it’s our duty of care, our contract there with the passenger. 100% our responsibility. We do not recover this money from anybody. (VO11) ATNS HAS BEEN SCRAMBLING TO GET THESE INSTRUMENT FLIGHT PROCEDURES RE-INSTATED WITH SOME SUCCESS, USING A HAND-AMENDED NOTICE TO AIRMAN OR AMOC TO UPDATE THE CHARTS. BUT AIRLINE CHIEFS REMAIN ANGRY, INCLUDING THE OUTGOING CEO OF AIRLINK, RODGER FOSTER. RODGER FOSTER: ATNS has created a serious safety risk, as airlines we are doing our best to mitigate it. Instrument flight procedures are fundamental to airline operational safety. (VO12) FOSTER DELIVERED A SCATHING SPEECH AS HE RETIRED, SAYING THAT HIS AIRLINE HAD BLED R55 MILLION IN THE LAST YEAR AS A RESULT OF STATE DYSFUNCTION. WE PUT THIS TO THE MINISTER OF TRANSPORT, BARBARA CREECY. MASA KEKANA: It was the former Airlink CEO who lambasted ATNS. He basically called it economic sabotage. BARBARA CREECY Transport Minister, GNU Yes, I saw his article. MASA KEKANA: What did you make of that? BARBARA CREECY Transport Minister, GNU: Well, he runs an airline. He's got a right to be angry. MASA KEKANA: Do you understand where he's coming from as well, in that frustration? BARBARA CREECY Transport Minister, GNU: Do you think I spend my time working on this day in and day out, because I take these problems lightly? And that’s why I've put in the intervention team. That's why I meet with them every second week, because I take them seriously (VO13) SINCE BEING SWORN INTO CABINET LAST YEAR, ATNS HAS BEEN ONE OF CREECY’S ONGOING HEADACHES. IN DECEMBER, SHE PARACHUTED A TEAM OF AVIATION EXPERTS INTO HEAD OFFICE TO DIAGNOSE THE PROBLEMS. SHE SANCTIONED REMEDIAL ACTION TO INCREASE SAFETY, FIX BROKEN TECHNOLOGY AND GET THE ATNS TRAINING SCHOOL RUNNING PROPERLY AGAIN. AND CRITICALLY, SHE BACKED A RECRUITMENT DRIVE BECAUSE KEY PERSONNEL - IN PARTICULAR AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS - WERE LEAVING IN DROVES. BARBARA CREECY Transport Minister, GNU South African Air Traffic controllers and also Flight Procedure Designers are extremely well trained, and they are in demand. And what we find is that developed countries can obviously offer much more in terms of packages than we are able to pay as a developing country. (VO14) AS THE GLOBAL AIR INDUSTRY’S RECOVERED AFTER COVID, SO HAS DEMAND FOR AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS. IN PLACES LIKE DUBAI, THEY CAN EARN UP TO THREE TO FOUR TIMES A MONTH WHAT THEY ARE OFFERED IN SOUTH AFRICA. IT’S A REASON WHY THIS YEAR’S WAGE NEGOTIATIONS IN ATNS WILL BE PARTICULARLY TOUGH, SAYS BAREND SMIT FROM THE LABOUR UNION SOLIDARITY. BAREND SMIT Union Representative, SOLIDARITY The salaries have been lagging behind for years and years. We are working with the public safety here, this is air traffic control. I think holding nice little media conferences and stuff isn't really going to change anything. The shareholder should simply reach into its pockets and see what they can give to these people who are leaving and make a plan. (VO15) THE SHAREHOLDER BEING A GOVERNMENT BATTLING TO MAKE ENDS MEET PIECE TO CAMERA MASA KEKANA: BETTER SALARIES ARE THE PULL – BUT THERE’S ALSO THE PUSH. A WHISTLEBLOWER’S LETTER ALLEGES THAT CRITICAL SKILLS HAVE BEEN CHASED AWAY FROM THE ORGANISATION IN A DISASTROUS RESTRUCTURING PROGRAMME. IT IS ALSO ALLEGES THAT AMONG THE NEW APPOINTMENTS ARE SOME OF THE BOSS’S FAMILY AND FRIENDS. (VO16) THESE DETAILED ALLEGATIONS GAVE AN INSIDE TRACK ON HOW ATNS, LED BY CEO NOZIPHO MDAWE, HAD BEEN HOBBLED BY INTERNAL PROBLEMS. THE SHAREHOLDER, THE MINISTER OF TRANSPORT, TOOK ACTION. BARBARA CREECY Transport Minister, GNU: There was an organizational redesign process, which we have put on hold as a result of this intervention. And this organizational redesign process was something that was not popular with the professional individuals. We have been so focused on the crisis, I haven't had an opportunity to consider: was this a good process or a bad process? But, it's been put on hold because this is a situation that is causing us to lose skilled personnel, and I wouldn't want us to lose any more skilled personnel at this point in time. (VO17) BUT THEN ANOTHER WHISTLEBLOWER’S LETTER FOLLOWED, DESCRIBING A TOXIC WORKPLACE, INCLUDING REFERENCES TO SEXUAL HARASSMENT, BULLYING, FAVOURITISM AND INCOMPETENCE. PIECE TO CAMERA MASA KEKANA: WE HAVE HAD CONVERSATIONS WITH AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS WHO HAVE LEFT ATNS AND THEY HAVE CONFIRMED THE LOW MORALE, AS WELL AS THE DIFFICULTIES OF DOING THEIR JOBS BECAUSE OF BROKEN INFRASTRUCTURE AND POOR MANAGEMENT. (VO16) ENTREPRENEUR MILES VAN DER MOLEN HEADS CEMAIR, A LOCAL AIRLINE WHICH TURNS TWENTY THIS YEAR. VAN DER MOLEN’S BEEN FLYING SINCE HE WAS A TEENAGER. HE IS CONCERNED ABOUT THE DEGRADATION OF THE ENTIRE AVIATION ECOSYSTEM, INCLUDING FUEL SHORTAGES, INFRASTRUCTURE COLLAPSE AND NOW ATNS. ALL THIS HURTS HIS BOTTOM LINE. MASA KEKANA: So if you're losing 10 million Rand in a matter of 12 months that wasn’t budgeted for, what has that done to your profits as an airline? Miles van der Molen, CEO, CemAir Airlines across South Africa have always been very marginal, and can see that by the number of failures over the decades. So it is really damaging. Of course, you have to price it in ultimately to your ticket price. So ultimately, what will result in is higher cost of flying in the hands of the consumer. MASA KEKANA: So more expensive tickets? MILES VAN DER MOLEN: Absolutely prices have to go up if the costs go up, it’s simply how that couple works. Upsound: The industry runs on confidence…. (VO17) AND IT’S NOT JUST THE FUEL BILL THAT COUNTS. THERE’S A KNOCK-ON EFFECT ON MULTIPLE PARTS OF THE OPERATION - AND THE LIVES OF THE PASSENGERS AND AIRLINE CREW. Miles van der Molen, CEO, CemAir If you have a severe delay in the morning and you may not be able to use the same crew as planned, you may need to get a new set of crew out to fly the aircraft for the later flight. You can end up with these runaway delays simply because to comply with the remaining regulations, significant logistical challenges present themselves. (VO17) WHEN WE FINALLY GOT TO SIT DOWN WITH THE ATNS BOARD CHAIRPERSON ZOLA MAJAVU, HE APOLOGISED TO AIRLINES AND THE PUBLIC. AND THEN GAVE A STARTLING INSIGHT INTO THE LOW MORALE AT ATNS. ZOLA MAJAVU Board Chairman, ATNS The board mandated me to do something unconventional, to descend to the level of operations, to say, you senior managers, get out of the way, maybe you are the reason why these people cannot talk. And I did station visits, and I spoke to all levels of management, and horrifying stuff was coming out. That place is toxic, it’s a snake pit. The ease with which people can paint each other with a whole host of allegations is shocking. (VO18) AT THE MINISTER’S REQUEST, THE BOARD SUSPENDED THE CEO, NOZIPHO MDAWE, AND IS CONDUCTING A RANGE OF INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATIONS, ALONGSIDE A PROBE BY THE PUBLIC PROTECTOR. MASA KEKANA: How did it get there? ZOLA MAJAVU, Board Chair, ATNS: It's been like that, even before we came a year and a bit in there. MASA KEKANA: So how do you clean up a toxic culture? ZOLA MAJAVU: We have even resorted to not investigating using internal processes that are there in terms of your statutory labor law, because today it’s this one, tomorrow, it's that one. Today, I lay a grievance against you. You lay a counter grievance. It's a mess. (VO19)OVER A LENGTHY INTERVIEW, MAJAVU AND HEAD OF OPERATIONS, CAINE MAINGANYA, PAINT A PICTURE OF AN SOE IN INTENSIVE CARE, GIVING A COMMITMENT THAT THEY ARE FIXING ATNS, WHATEVER IT TAKES. ZOLA MAJAVU, Board Chair, ATNS: Every single week the board submits a progress report to the Minister. I sign it every Monday because we want to keep our fingers on the pulse all the time because of complacency in some instances. We are making sure that we are keeping them on their toes, every week, every week. (VO20) PART OF THIS RENEWAL IS AN AGGRESSIVE RECRUITMENT CAMPAIGN TO MAKE UP STAFF SHORTAGES, PARTICULARLY THE GAPS AT THE BUSIEST AIRPORTS CAINE MAINGANYA Head of Operations, ATNS The example of OR Tambo, for example, we are sitting at about 70% staffing, We're sitting at about 80% staffing in Cape Town and in King Shaka, we also have made great strides at about 90% so those are generally the areas where we're seeing the most impact. (VO21)THEY ALSO COMMITTED TO HAVE THE FLIGHT PROCEDURES SORTED BY THE END OF NEXT YEAR. PIECE TO CAMERA MASA KEKANA: SOUTH AFRICANS NEED TO FLY FOR BUSINESS AND PLEASURE OUR ECONOMY DEPENDS ON IT. AND THE AIRLINES ARE THE GEESE THAT DELIVER THE GOLDEN EGGS AND THEY WANT TO BE HEARD… (VO22) THE AIRLINE ASSOCIATION IS COUNTING THE COSTS OF THE FAILURES OF ATNS. MUNETSI SAYS MORE THAN A QUARTER OF ALL FLIGHTS ARE BEHIND TIME WHICH IS BAD FOR BUSINESS, UNDERMINES TOURISM AND THE ECONOMY IN GENERAL, AND THREATENS THE FUTURE OF THE AVIATION INDUSTRY. Aaron Munetsi CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa: The airlines unfortunately bear the brunt. They are not compensated. The airlines also have to pay their air traffic navigation services fees. If they don't pay, they are grounded, so they pay the fees for a service that they don't receive. MASA KEKANA: How is the industry coping with all this? Aaron Munetsi CEO, Airlines Association of Southern Africa: We're a very resilient industry but we are really, really stretched to the max. SOUNDUP: Stow your hand luggage securely and ensure your seatbelts are fastened, we will be on our way shortly. (VO23) WHILE ATNS AND THE MINISTER SAY THEY ARE WORKING HARD TO FIX THESE DEVASTATING PROBLEMS, CemAir HAS BEEN OPERATING IN OTHER REGIONS, TO OFFSET THE RISK OF FLYING IN SOUTH AFRICA, LEASING OUT AIRCRAFT AROUND THE WORLD. Miles van der Molen, CEO, CemAir It's exciting and sad, you know, we get a lot of people comment on seeing a South African aircraft in the Caribbean, and it does create opportunities for South Africans who operate those aircraft, but it certainly decreases the choices consumers have in this market for flight options.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We expose the growing risk in air safety in South Africa as a result of a crisis at the heart of the Air Traffic Navigation Service
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We are able to pull together the complex picture of air safety in South Africa, narrated by industry players outside of the organisation charged with ensuring that safety, the ATNS, as well as from inside the agency which has been failing to meet its deadlines and is compromised by allegations of disfunction.
metadata.Summary: It appears that South Africa’s safety guardians of the sky have been in trouble for some years – at least critically from 2017 when as the industry insiders say the “cracks began to show”. However, those cracks became a chasm in July 2023 when vital safety instruments were suspended by the regulatory body the, the South African Civil Aviation Authority, SACAA. https://www.caa.co.za. These procedures create the legal route for aircraft to land and take-off from South Africa's airports, and if they are not properly sanctioned and administered, the safety risk increases dramatically, and in some instances, scheduled flights can not take off or land, causing delay and huge financial penalties to airlines and passengers, and the economy as a whole.
metadata.Further information: This complex problem needs to be explained to be understood as it is a technical element of flying. EXPLAINING PROCEDURES All airplanes need to follow premapped routes to leave airports and land on them. These are called Procedures. There are IFP – Instrument Flight Procedures – and VFP’s Visual Flight Procedures/Rules. International global agreements underpin the conventions of air safety and travel, and this way of mapping take-off and landing are part of those conventions and are called Procedures. Instrument Flight Procedures are conducted through the instruments in the cockpit. Visual Flight Procedures are from looking out of the window. And they are required to be renewed every five years. South Africa has 326 procedures for its main airports and in July 2023 they were suspended because they had expired. The reason why they have to be renewed is because the terrain around the airports changes over time. And there needs to be a legal route that all airplanes take as they arrive and take off depending on the wind to ensure they don’t bump into each other or through pilot error they don’t crash in to anything. Until 2023, South Africa mostly had had these procedures in place. The effect of NOT having these procedures in place is that if the weather is bad and a plane needs to land using one of these procedures, they will NOT be able to land and have to divert or circle, depending on how much fuel they have on board. The cost of diverting is potentially big, not just for the airline but also for the passengers who may be preparing to catch connecting flights, take a holiday, be at a meeting, deliver a widget, pharmaceuticals etc. BACK TO THE STORY The CAA then gave the ATNS an extension of a year to get their Procedures in order. They failed to come to the party and map those procedures. It appears that this failure was in part due to a toxic turmoil within the organisation which chased away skilled employees, and placed less skilled junior employees in their place. Not only were Air Traffic controllers leaving in droves, but the people skilled enough to design the procedures were also leaving. Two whistleblower letters have been sent to the Minister of Transport and unions to complain about a raft of issues, which seem pretty standard in troubled SOEs – cronyism, incompetence, toxicity and a particular type of transformation which favours the well-connected. I have read the whistleblower letters – many of the commentators I have spoken to argue that they can not be relied on hundred per cent to tell the truth, but they are suggestive a basked of real problems. So much so that it attracted the attention of the Minister of Transport herself, Barbara Creecy. A SOLUTION FOUND – AND THEN REJECTED In the midst of the story which broke as a result of the ATNS missing its next deadline in July 2024, a solution was found in the appointment of a Swedish company which works in the Air Traffic Navigation Space Globally, IBG. https://ibg.aero This is a big professional global company with clients in the big flight centres of the world. The person they tasked to lead the pitch for work was a former South African air traffic controller, now in living in the UK, who has asked to be kept anonymous but with whom I spoke to this week. IBG Aero offered to help train up the flight procedure designers that were there and help ATNS do all the procedures before the Christmas holidays. A contract was signed and a letter of appointment sent to them. But shortly after that happened, ATNS decided to do due diligence on its offering. IBG sent them the names of the designers and their CVs. They came from SkyGuide which is the Swiss version of ATNS. The COO of ATNS, Josia Monyakoana, said they did not meet the standards that were required and rejected them. IBG sent the certificates of the designers they would deploy as proof of their abilities, and Mr Monyakoana said he did not trust the certificates, because they did not itemise the skills the designers had learnt on the courses which awarded them the certificates. So there was a series of to and fro with the IBG people – who had been to Johannesburg to prepare for the work – which has led to stalemate. All this I have now got from two sources, one of whom was in the negotiations. WHY – DID THE CHIEF DESIGNER HAVE SOMETHING TO DO WITH IT? While this was taking place, the newly appointed acting external Chief Designer of ATNS, Vuyo Kela, was setting up her own Aviation Consultancy company, while taking up the position of the most highly paid chief designer. She was a former employee of ATNS, had been working in Dubai, and had come back to South Africa looking for work. Josia Monyakoana was her referee on her CV of two years ago. The whistleblower letter alleges that Mr Monyakoana and Mr Kwela could be a romantic item, but I have no evidence of this. Nor have I found any trace of her company online, PWV Aviation Consultants, beyond her Linked In profile. So at this point, my evidence of this part of the story is hearsay, and what I am told off the record which is speculative and could be framed to some degree by the whistelblowers letters. Two people I spoke to raised the issues of sexual harassment as part of the toxic culture of ATNS and how senior executives prey on younger women traffic controllers or staff. This is also mentioned in the whistleblower’s letters. I have found evidence of this story in a recent scandal in Feb 2025 of ATNS air traffic boss demanding oral sex and other activities, including spanking, from a junior. https://sundayworld.co.za/news/black-business-council-demands-suspension-of-sex-pest-boss/ https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/media-statement-sexual-harassment-allegations-under-investigation-gzkwf/?trackingId=CweG%2F12eTlaG52%2BV%2FpqZ5A%3D%3D Apparently there are other incidences but nothing online that I can find. The whistleblower’s letter list this and other issues building a case that ATNS has become dysfunctional and is run as a fiefdom of Josia Manyakoana and Vuyo Kwela. The first whistleblower’s letter was released on the 18th of September 2024. It goes into detail giving the background of the people who were brought in by the new CEO, Nozipho Portia Mdawe, who came from Transnet National Ports Authority and knew very little about aviation. It complains that she brought in friends from Transnet, tried to get outside consultancies to compensate for the lack of knowledge of the highly paid newcomers, and pushed out expertise in the name of transformation. It concludes by calling for an investigation into 8 people who were appointed by Ms Mdawe and a number of other issues. The letter was addressed to the Minister Barbara Creecy and the unions and it was leaked to the media, all before the debacle with IBG. As a result of the pressure, including quiet pressure from airlines, the Minister swooped in and suspended Ms Ndawo and sent in a three-person intervention team of former employees to try and stabilise the situation. There was a promise of the inclusion of a vendor (IBG of above) to help fix things and the less sceptical breathed a sign of relief. But by March this year, it became clear that things were not fixing themselves despite all the hand holding. The Minister cranked up the pressure and held a press conference on the 14th of March at ATNS. She said she had now asked the intervention team to physically go into the offices daily. She claimed recruitment of procedure designers was going well and success was had in coaxing back procedure designers and flight controllers. Many have left for the Middle East or elsewhere in desperation. She herself appears to be taking personal responsibility for this as much as she can, within her ministerial ambit. However, days after her press conference another whistleblower letter was released saying the Minister had had her facts wrong, that the ATNS was pulling wool over her eyes and that further symptoms of managerial dysfunction were undermining the work of the people who were meant to be keeping the aeroplanes and passengers safe. One of the fights is over the unequal distribution of retainer bonuses across the country. This last whistleblowers letter claims that: In Nov 2024 Four Tower controllers left In Dec 2024 Four radar controllers left In Feb 2025 the tower pool manager left More than six area controllers have left for Dubai It’s difficult to properly quantify these numbers but it seems dire. They also say that since Josia Manyakoana took over as COO five flight procedure specialist have left the company, with only one left, (and I think she has now left as well and is working as a consultant from outside) Also the training has been delayed because there are only two instructors left and Vuyo Kela is allegedly refusing to hire in anybody, except her friends. She is apparently also managing recruitment and a number of other appointments. At the same time, I have been told that the Presidency (not sure why) has added to the list of responsibilities of ATNS the job of mapping all the wind turbines in South Africa. They do not have the staff or capacity for this. It falls under Obstacle Evaluations. https://atns.com/uncategorized/wind-farm-application/8310/ There is now growing panic in the aviation services and the community around ATNS, although ATNS’s leaders are not necessarily expressing such. In a hastily convened meeting this week, ATNS leaders told airline executives that they had amended the procedures through an AMOC ( an alternative method of compliance) by writing notes to the maps, to give the airlines a route to land and take off at most of the airports. There is some doubt as to how legal that is, although an AMOC is a recognised procedure. There is concern that this has been done in order to make it possible for the G20 to land at George to go Fancourt for a meeting. Three airports have been left out – they haven’t got to their procedures yet – Bloemfontein, Upington and Richard’s Bay. That means scheduled aircraft can’t land if the weather is bad, if I read the press release correctly. It also appears that the weather is often blamed for an ability of a plane to land, when in fact it is the case of the procedure being missing. If that procedure had been place, despite clouds, the aircraft would have landed. While people have a lot to say about this off the record, it’s very difficult to get commentators to say all of this on the record. I have had enough off the record conversations to be convinced that ATNS is in serious trouble and that this is impacting on the safety and financial viability of the airline industry. But it’s not possible to test all those allegations in such a short period of time, and we would need a strategy to deal with the whistleblower’s report. There are a lot of angry airmen out there – and everybody is concerned. Except of course, it appears, the Chief Operating Officer himself, Josia Manyokoana and his Chief Designer, Vuyo Kela. However our requests to interview Mr Manyakoana are being rebuffed and we have been given a lesser staff member to interview in Caine Mainganya. When I asked for an interview for the COO, Mr Manyakoana, for the third time in writing, I got this: The COO is hands-on, overseeing the implementation of the entire ATNS Instrument Flight Procedure Maintenance Programme. It would be unfair to him to redirect his energies to something else, other than focusing in ensuring that our airspace is safe - at all times. At the bottom of ATNS’s website it says: We are always looking for talented people to join our organisation. Apply now and become part of our unique culture. Against these revelations, that seems ironic.
